title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: "The assistant only retrieves what the asking user can already see." How should you read that? `[V]`
options: As a vendor claim that should be independently verified before deployment
As true and reassuring — it means the assistant introduces no new exposure
As true and as the entire problem, because it means the assistant inherits your existing access model including every mistake in it
As false — assistants index content beyond individual user permissions
questions.explanation: Both halves have to be held at once. No new access is created; every over-share you already had becomes one prompt away, because the effort that was hiding it does not survive.

questions.prompt: Why is "this is a permissions problem, not an AI problem" an inadequate response?
options: Because it is factually incorrect
Because it is true and settles nothing — the permissions problem was survivable at the old discovery cost and is not survivable at the new one
Because permissions and AI risk cannot be separated technically
Because it shifts responsibility to IT, who will refuse it
questions.explanation: "AI didn't cause this" is true and is not a defence. Removing the friction that made a latent problem tolerable is a change in kind, even though nothing in the access model moved.

questions.prompt: What makes HR's corpus a worse case than other functions'?
options: HR documents are more numerous than other functions' documents
The ratio of restricted to routine content is higher than anywhere else — and the subjects of the documents are employees who hold assistant licences
HR documents are less likely to be correctly labelled
HR systems have weaker access controls than finance systems
questions.explanation: Finance holds sensitive aggregates; HR holds sensitive individuals, and those individuals are inside your tenant asking in good faith about their own situation. Which is why generic rollout guidance, sized for a mostly-routine corpus, under-serves you invisibly.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that summarization "launders provenance"?
options: That the assistant removes metadata from documents it processes
That the answer contains a document's substance with no filename, no permission prompt, no access event, and no audit entry — because the user read an answer rather than a document
That summaries are harder to classify than source documents
That the assistant cannot cite its sources reliably
questions.explanation: Which breaks the assumption every permission model rests on: that finding something is work, and that the last step of finding it leaves a record.

questions.prompt: Which consequence of provenance laundering does the module say causes the most trouble?
options: That leak investigations will find no file access
That the user is not culpable, so there is no deterrent
That aggregation across partially-reachable sources produces facts no single document contained, which are therefore in nobody's index of sensitive material
That audit logs cannot be reconciled
questions.explanation: Three partially-reachable sources can yield who is being managed out. Nobody over-shared that; the assistant assembled it, and it did not exist until it was asked for. A and B are real and listed below it.

questions.prompt: Why does the module recommend exclusion before sensitivity labelling?
options: Because labelling requires licences that exclusion does not
Because labelling only protects you to the extent it is correct, and yours is not yet — while the most reliable protection for a document is not being in the index
Because labels can be removed by document owners
Because exclusion is required for regulatory compliance
questions.explanation: Labelling at the source is the better long-term control and the wrong first move. The principle mirrors the Comp & Benefits track's rule that the most reliable protection for a data element is its absence.

questions.prompt: Why is testing the assistant as yourself the discipline's most common error? `[V]`
options: Because administrators receive different model behaviour than standard users
Because you are an administrator who can see everything, so every result you get is reassuring and means nothing — the vendor's own guidance is to validate exposure per persona
Because admin accounts are excluded from audit logging
Because your queries are cached differently
questions.explanation: The fix is concrete: obtain a test account with the permissions of a mid-level individual contributor with no HR role, and ask it the ten questions you would least like answered.

questions.prompt: For a practitioner who does not administer the assistant tenant, what does the module recommend?
options: Escalating the risk in writing and treating it as another function's problem
Requesting administrative access so the work can be done properly
Authoring the exclusion list — the artifact only this role can write, since nobody in IT knows which site holds redundancy selections — and bringing the list rather than the concern
Delaying any assistant deployment until permissions are remediated
questions.explanation: A concern gets acknowledged and filed; a list of named sites with a sentence each converts your problem into their ten-minute configuration task. A is the position the module's counter-argument defends, and the write-up has to engage it.
